title: Hollywood, Los Angeles
description: Neighborhood in Los Angeles, California, US
wiki_lead:
Hollywood, sometimes informally called Tinseltown, is a neighborhood in Central Los Angeles, California. Its name has become synonymous with the American film industry and the people associated with it. Despite this association, most major film studios are located outside the neighborhood, although Paramount Pictures maintains a studio lot within it.
Hollywood was incorporated as an independent municipality on November 9, 1903. The municipality was consolidated with the City of Los Angeles on February 7, 1910 following a referendum.
wiki_excerpt:
Hollywood, sometimes informally called Tinseltown, is a neighborhood in Central Los Angeles, California. Its name has become synonymous with the American film industry and the people associated with it. Despite this association, most major film studios are located outside the neighborhood, although Paramount Pictures maintains a studio lot within it.
Hollywood was incorporated as an independent municipality on November 9, 1903. The municipality was consolidated with the City of Los Angeles on February 7, 1910 following a referendum.


History


Initial development

H. J. Whitley, a real estate developer, arranged to buy the 480-acre (1.9 km2) E.C. Hurd ranch. Whitley shared his plans for the new town with General Harrison Gray Otis, publisher of the Los Angeles Times, and Ivar Weid, a prominent businessman in the area.
Daeida Wilcox, who donated land to help in the development of Hollywood, learned of the name Hollywood from an acquaintance who owned an estate by that name in Illinois.
Wilcox is quoted as saying, "I chose the name Hollywood simply because it sounds nice and because I'm superstitious and holly brings good luck."  She recommended the same name to her husband, Harvey H. Wilcox, who had purchased 120 acres on February 1, 1887. It was not until August 1887 that Wilcox decided to use that name and filed with the Los Angeles County Recorder's office on a deed and parcel map of the property.
By 1900, the region had a post office, newspaper, hotel, and two markets. Los Angeles, with a population of 102,479, lay 10 miles (16 km) east through the vineyards, barley fields, and citrus groves. A single-track streetcar line ran down the middle of Prospect Avenue from it, but service was infrequent and the trip took two hours. The old citrus fruit-packing house was converted into a livery stable, improving transportation for the inhabitants of Hollywood.
The Hollywood Hotel was opened in 1902 by Whitley, president of the Los Angeles Pacific Boulevard and Development Company. Having finally acquired the Hurd ranch and subdivided it, Whitley built the hotel to attract land buyers. Flanking the west side of Highland Avenue, the structure fronted on Prospect Avenue (later Hollywood Boulevard). Although it was still a dusty, unpaved road, it was regularly graded and graveled. The hotel became internationally known and was the center of civic and social life and home of movie stars for many years.
Whitley's company developed and sold one of the early residential areas, the Ocean View Tract. Whitley did much to promote the area. He paid thousands of dollars to install electricity and arrange for electric lighting, and he built both a bank and a road into the Cahuenga Pass. The lighting ran for several blocks down Prospect Avenue. Whitley's land was centered on Highland Avenue. His 1918 development, Whitley Heights, was named for him.

grok_lead: Hollywood is a neighborhood in the central region of Los Angeles, California, historically established as the epicenter of the American motion picture industry and synonymous with global cinema production. Originally subdivided as a residential tract in 1887 by Harvey H. Wilcox, the area derived its name from an estate encountered by his wife, Daeida Wilcox, during travel, evoking images of lush holly groves. Incorporated as an independent municipality in 1903, Hollywood consolidated with Los Angeles in 1910 primarily to access the larger city's water infrastructure amid growth pressures. The neighborhood's defining transformation occurred in the early 20th century when filmmakers migrated from the East Coast, attracted by consistent sunlight, diverse landscapes, and relatively inexpensive land, establishing pioneering studios like Nestor Film Company in 1911. This influx catalyzed the creation of a vertically integrated studio system, producing thousands of films that shaped popular culture and exported American narratives worldwide, with Hollywood outputting over 80% of U.S. feature films by the 1920s. Iconic landmarks emerged, including the Hollywood Sign âoriginally erected in 1923 as " Hollywoodland " to promote real estate âand the Hollywood Walk of Fame, honoring contributions to entertainment since 1958. While retaining cultural prestige through awards like the Oscars and tourist draws generating billions in economic activity, Hollywood has encountered controversies including labor disputes, creative monopolization by major studios, and a perceptible ideological uniformity in output that critics attribute to institutional biases within the industry. Recent empirical trends reveal contraction, with motion picture employment in Los Angeles County plummeting from 142,000 in 2022 to around 100,000 by 2024, driven by production shifts to tax-incentivized locales, streaming disruptions, and post-pandemic recoveries lagging national averages.
